source.title: Revisiting the Train Loss: an Efficient Performance Estimator for Neural Architecture Search
source.authors: Robin Ru; Clare Lyle; Lisa Schut; M. Fil; Mark van der Wilk; Yarin Gal

record.file_problem: Supplied text is titled “Speedy Performance Estimation for Neural Architecture Search,” while the provided title is “Revisiting the Train Loss: an Efficient Performance Estimator for Neural Architecture Search.” The text is otherwise a complete paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether training-trajectory loss measures predict final test performance across architecture search settings. It does not test the specific behaviors in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates rank correlations between early training-loss estimators and final test accuracy, including comparisons with validation-based estimators. These findings bear on the broader subject but do not measure the specific behaviors named in V1–V8. Values used to select estimator settings are not separate results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates training-loss summaries as predictors of architecture rankings under fixed training setups. Its results do not test any V1–V8 behavior. Training-speed prediction is distinct from V7's magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization-gap comparison; varying NAS setups also does not isolate optimizer, batch-size, or dropout effects.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that early training-loss sums efficiently estimate final architecture-performance rankings and improve several NAS procedures. They restrict prediction to architectures compared under fixed training hyperparameters and acknowledge that validation accuracy eventually becomes preferable with sufficient training.
record.recipe_differences: Uses early training-loss trajectories to rank architectures by final test accuracy; it does not reproduce the random-label, width, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example tests in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Estimator performance varies with training budget and estimator variant; the paper reports reduced effectiveness when architectures begin to overfit. It states that cross-hyperparameter prediction was outside scope.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-loss estimators TSE and TSE-E outperform corresponding validation-loss estimators in ranking sampled NASBench-201 architectures by final test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-loss trajectory summaries can predict relative final test performance among architectures trained under a fixed setup.

fits_no_version.finding: The three CIFAR100 examples illustrate divergence between validation loss and validation accuracy, but inconsistent B/C accuracy assignments prevent confirming the claimed perfect training-loss ranking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Validation-loss rankings can disagree with validation-accuracy rankings across architectures.

record.problems: The central comparisons concern rank correlation among architectures, not train-test error gaps of individual trained networks. Several central figure results have no exact values in the text. The supplied C.2 example gives accuracy values inconsistent with its stated ranking.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numeric rows were extracted from plots whose values are not stated in text. Table 2 reports one-shot NAS estimator comparisons and top-10 architecture accuracy, but those evaluate the estimator in a NAS procedure rather than the claim’s generalization-gap behaviors.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and random-label held-out chance performance under matched recipes.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization, local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including tuning, weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Large-batch held-out penalties under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that remove them.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across data sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the reader's tests/T2 classification to discusses/T6. Citing Jiang et al. for optimization-speed measures does not test V7. No additional results bearing on V1–V8 require missing rows.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error as network width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD generalization under different tuning regimes.
Large-batch generalization gaps and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: Three example architectures (Arch A, Arch B, Arch C)
rows.operation_detail: Compared training loss, validation loss, and validation accuracy.
rows.measure: Training loss; validation loss; validation accuracy
rows.note: Authors state the training-loss ranking corresponds perfectly (negatively) with validation-accuracy ranking, while validation-loss ranking is poorly or wrongly correlated. The accuracy ordering in the supplied text conflicts with the listed values for Arch B and Arch C, so the three-way ranking is not resolved here.
rows.check: An illustrative comparison of three architectures, not a test of V1–V8. Figure 7 captions give validation accuracies A=0.70, B=0.64, C=0.67, whereas the prose assigns B=0.67 and C=0.64. The claimed perfect inverse ordering with training loss therefore cannot be established consistently. The row also combines three subjects and three measures.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
